findings.title: Multiple-provider check removed; equal-order providers are now silently resolved
findings.body: `detectProvider` used to fail fast when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, so a misconfigured deployment (for example default and FIPS together) no longer fails. Stable sorting then makes the winner depend on ServiceLoader/classpath order, and the ignored providers are only listed at DEBUG. `ServiceLoader` is also drained eagerly, so every provider is instantiated, including those that are then ignored. The `FIPS1402Provider` and `DefaultCryptoProvider` constructors have global side effects (`Security.insertProviderAt`, `Security.addProvider`). Equal-order ties should still throw, or the fallback should be the only case where multiple providers are tolerated. At minimum, log a WARN when the top two orders are equal.

findings.title: `order()` added as an abstract interface method breaks existing implementations
findings.body: `CryptoProvider` is a public SPI. Adding `int order()` without a default makes every external or third-party implementation, and any test or custom provider elsewhere in the repo not updated here, fail to compile. It also fails at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` against already-built jars. A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep source and binary compatibility and still let the built-in providers override it.

findings.title: Dead code: two ASN1 encodings are computed and discarded
findings.body: `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` build encoders and throw the results away. The real encoding is built again in the `writeDerSeq(...)` call below. These lines do nothing and look like leftover debugging. Remove them.

findings.title: No input validation in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: The method assumes `signature.length >= signLength`. If the input is shorter, `System.arraycopy` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, an unchecked exception, although the method contract declares `IOException`. Callers that handle malformed signatures through `IOException` will not catch it. Check the length and throw `IOException`.

findings.title: Signature, KeyFactory, KeyPairGenerator and related operations throw UnsupportedOperationException
findings.body: `getSignature`, `getKeyFactory`, `getKeyPairGen`, `getAesCbcCipher`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getPemUtils` and others all throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. `AuthzClient.create` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init`, which picks this provider whenever it is the only one on the classpath. Any authz-client flow that needs JWS signing, for example `client-jwt`/`signed-jwt` client credentials or ES/RS signature handling in keycloak-core, will then fail at runtime with a bare 'Not supported yet.' None of these methods even use the JDK's default providers, which would be enough for RSA/EC signatures. The limitation is not documented in the class Javadoc.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JDK provider (SUN) via a KeyStore lookup
findings.body: The method returns whatever provider backs the default KeyStore type, normally `SUN`, not BouncyCastle. Code that derives its provider name from this (for example `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` used in `Signature.getInstance(alg, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)`) will look up algorithms in `SUN`, which does not provide RSA/EC signatures or AES ciphers. This produces confusing `NoSuchAlgorithmException`/`NoSuchProviderException` failures. The result also depends on the `keystore.type` security property. Returning `null` (as the Elytron provider does) or documenting the intent would be safer.

findings.title: Indefinite/negative length is not handled and surfaces as NegativeArraySizeException
findings.body: `readLength()` returns -1 for the indefinite-length marker (0x80). `readInteger()` then calls `read(length)` and `readNext()` calls `read(length + header)`. For a malformed or indefinite-length element these reach `new byte[negative]` in `read(int)`, which throws an unchecked `NegativeArraySizeException`. The method signatures promise `IOException`, so callers will not handle it. Reject length < 0 with an `IOException` (DER does not allow indefinite lengths). Also, `readSequence` does not check that the declared length is consumed exactly or that no trailing data follows.

findings.title: Round-trip-only test with a P-256 key for all algorithms; no fixed vectors or edge cases
findings.body: The test generates one default EC key (P-256) and signs with ES256, ES384 and ES512 using that same key. The ES384/ES512 cases therefore only exercise the padding branch of `integerToBytes` with 32-byte r/s, not real P-384/P-521 signatures. The assertion only compares RS→DER→RS with the encoder and decoder from the same class, so a consistent bug in both would pass. It never asserts that `asn1Des` equals the original JDK DER signature, and it never verifies the re-encoded signature with `Signature.verify`. The random key also means the interesting edge cases (r or s with a leading zero byte, or with the high bit set) are not tested deterministically. Nothing tests the new `order()`/provider selection in `CryptoIntegration` either.
